extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent applicants (U.S. subject-matter eligibility for nature-based inventions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on analyzing 35 U.S.C. § 101 subject-matter eligibility for nature-based products (e.g., bacteria, nucleic acids, antibodies, cells, food mixtures), using the two-step framework (statutory category check; judicial-exception/marked-difference and 'significantly more' analyses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation for claim analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are analyzed for eligibility in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the broadest reasonable interpretation when determining whether claims fall into statutory categories and when assessing whether they are directed to a judicial exception or include additional elements that add significantly more. Examples throughout the guidance use this interpretive standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Statutory category check
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a statutory category (e.g., composition of matter, process, machine, or manufacture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is not directed to any statutory category, it fails Step 1. If it is directed to a statutory category, proceed to the judicial-exception analysis (Step 2A). Examples: the guidance treats compositions of matter (bacteria, nucleic acids, antibodies, cells, food compositions) as statutory categories (Step 1: YES).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — Judicial exception: product of nature analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception such as a 'product of nature' (i.e., whether it claims something that exists in nature). For nature-based products, use the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis to decide if the claimed product is an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed nature-based product is not markedly different from its natural counterpart, the claim is directed to a product-of-nature exception (Step 2A: YES) and proceeds to Step 2B. If it is markedly different, it is not directed to the exception (Step 2A: NO) and qualifies as eligible subject matter. Examples: bacterial mixtures, nucleic acids, antibodies, cells, foods are analyzed under this test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics (core criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed nature-based product must have 'markedly different characteristics' (structural, functional, or other) compared to its naturally occurring counterpart to avoid being a product-of-nature exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics may be structural (sequence, chemical bonds, single-molecule vs. separate molecules), functional (new biological activities, infectivity, expression patterns, growth rates), or other observable differences. Examples: (i) a bacterial combination that causes one species to infect a new plant species; (ii) nucleic acid sequence substitutions or labels that change function or structure; (iii) vectors combining heterologous sequences; (iv) chimeric/humanized/variant antibodies; (v) cells with induced phenotypic changes (marker expression, increased oxygen utilization); (vi) mixed cell populations with interacting cells producing new biological properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation alone is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely isolating a natural product from its native environment (e.g., severing chemical bonds to remove a gene from a chromosome) does not necessarily make it markedly different from the naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolated but otherwise unchanged nucleic acids (same nucleotide sequence) are not markedly different under Myriad and are ineligible. Similarly, man-made products identical to naturally occurring products (e.g., isolated cells with the same genotype and phenotype) do not meet the marked-difference test. The fact of isolation without additional modifications does not avoid the product-of-nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that encompass natural and non-natural embodiments — effect on eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim covers both embodiments that are identical to what exists in nature and embodiments that are changed, the claim can be directed to a product-of-nature exception because it encompasses natural embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim to 'an antibody to Protein S' that covers naturally occurring murine or coyote antibodies as well as engineered antibodies fails the marked-difference test because at least some embodiments are identical to nature. Narrowing the claim (e.g., to human antibodies, specific CDR sequences, chimeric/humanized antibodies, or variant Fc domains) can render it eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixtures/aggregates: unchanged aggregation vs. synergistic/altered interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of natural components that merely aggregates them without changing their characteristics is a product-of-nature exception; by contrast, a combination that causes components to exhibit new characteristics (structural or functional) can be markedly different and eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (i) Aggregating different Rhizobium strains that remain unchanged and do not alter each species' use is ineligible (Funk Brothers). (ii) A particular mixture where one species acquires the ability to infect an additional plant species is markedly different and eligible. Likewise, a yogurt starter in which two bacterial species act synergistically to speed fermentation and reduce fat content is an instance where combination-induced properties can support marked difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nucleic acid-specific markers of marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in nucleic acid sequence or composition can provide marked differences from naturally occurring genes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-naturally occurring substitution modifications (e.g., at least one nucleotide changed from the native SEQ ID) that alter structural characteristics (sequence) and potentially functional characteristics (encoded protein, transcription/splicing) can be markedly different. Attaching labels (fluorescent/radioactive) to make a single labeled molecule that does not occur in nature, and vectors that combine the gene with heterologous sequences (viral promoters, sequences from other organisms) are examples of structural/functional differences that support eligibility. By contrast, an isolated nucleic acid with the same sequence as the natural gene but merely removed from its chromosome is not markedly different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antibody-specific markers of marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting antibody claims to non-naturally occurring antibodies or engineered changes can establish marked differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims limited to human antibodies (where no human antibodies to the antigen occur naturally), to antibodies defined by specific CDR sequences (e.g., SEQ ID NOs), to chimeric or humanized antibodies (fusion proteins combining parts of different species), or to antibodies comprising engineered variant Fc domains (amino acid modifications) are treated as having different structural and/or functional characteristics and thus can be eligible. A broad claim to 'an antibody' that includes naturally occurring antibodies fails the marked-difference test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cell-specific markers of marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Phenotypic or functional changes in cells caused by human manipulation can render cells markedly different from naturally occurring counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (i) man-made pacemaker cells that express a non-naturally occurring marker (marker Z) and exhibit increased oxygen utilization; (ii) cell populations with specified ratios (e.g., 10-15% marker Z / 85-90% marker P) where cells interact to change growth rates; these demonstrate biological property differences that rise to marked difference. By contrast, isolated man-made cells genetically and phenotypically identical to natural cells are not markedly different. The presence of containers alone (generic flasks, petri dishes) is routine and does not change the analysis unless the container/combination produces a non-routine improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — 'Significantly more' analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES), determine whether the claim as a whole includes additional elements or combinations that amount to 'significantly more' than the exception such that the claim is eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements that are well-understood, routine, and conventional (e.g., generic containers) do not add significantly more. Recitations at a high level of generality that merely instruct practitioners to use known techniques typically fail Step 2B. Conversely, combinations or specific limitations that confine the claim to a particular useful application and demonstrably improve the relevant technology (e.g., scaffold+cells that facilitate faster tissue regeneration) can amount to 'significantly more' and render the claim eligible. The analysis asks whether any element or combination ensures the claim amounts to more than the judicial exception itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic laboratory steps or well-understood elements do not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine, conventional laboratory practices (e.g., isolating cells, placing cells in generic containers) do not supply the 'significantly more' needed to transform a claim directed to a product-of-nature into eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim reciting a population of cells 'in a container' is insufficient when the container is recited at a high level of generality and is normally used in the art. Such recitations merely tell a scientist to use existing, routine equipment and therefore add nothing significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific combination elements can add 'significantly more' if they improve technology or confine application
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim element or combination that is not routine and that confines the claim to a particular useful application or improves a technological field may supply 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: pacemaker cells combined with a biocompatible three-dimensional scaffold (not general container) that facilitates faster tissue regeneration and is not merely routine can render the claim 'significantly more' and eligible. The scaffold plus cells provided a specific improvement in regenerative medicine rather than a generic linking of elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility that nature might randomly create a claimed molecule does not bar eligibility absent evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere theoretical possibility that nature could randomly produce a molecule similar to a claimed, human-made molecule does not render the claimed composition nonpatentable; the examiner must show that the claimed molecule actually exists in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Myriad: the possibility that nature might randomly create a similar molecule does not render a composition nonpatentable (emphasis: unless examiner can show existence in nature). Thus, claims limited to molecules not shown to exist in nature can be eligible even if theoretic random occurrence is conceivable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funk Brothers principle — discovery of natural quality is not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovering that natural strains or species have certain qualities (e.g., non-inhibition) and packaging them together without altering their properties is not patentable subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant's discovery of natural properties and the mere application/aggregation of those properties (e.g., selecting non-inhibitive strains and packaging them as an inoculant) is considered an application of nature's handiwork and may fail the marked-difference test. The aggregation produces no new organisms, no structural change, and no enlargement of utility; such claims were held ineligible in Funk Brothers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture existence in nature — burden on examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: If an examiner asserts a claimed mixture exists in nature and uses that to deny marked difference, the examiner must show that the particular mixture exists in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the components could theoretically occur together in nature, eligibility is not negated unless the examiner can demonstrate that the claimed particular mixture actually exists in nature. Reference: Myriad footnote and examples where absence of proof of natural occurrence supports eligibility.
